claim: Zfp281 protein is nuclear-localized and detected at low levels throughout the inner cell mass (ICM) and trophectoderm (TE) at E3.5 (mid-blastocyst stage).
source: At E3.5, representing the mid-blastocyst stage, Zfp281 was nuclear-localized and detected at low levels throughout the inner cell mass (ICM) and trophectoderm (TE) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Widespread Zfp281 expression is maintained until the late blastocyst stage (E4.5) in both ICM derivatives including Epi and PrE, as well as the TE.
source: This widespread expression was maintained until the late blastocyst stage (E4.5) in both ICM derivatives including Epi and PrE, as well as the TE (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Zfp281 expression is elevated in the epiblast of late stage blastocysts.
source: Single-cell quantitative immunofluorescence (Lou et al., 2014; Saiz et al., 2016) and single-cell microarray data (Ohnishi et al., 2014) revealed that Zfp281 expression was elevated in the epiblast of late stage blastocysts (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell quantitative immunofluorescence and single-cell microarray data from cited studies

claim: At post-implantation stages, Zfp281 expression is restricted to the epiblast and its derivatives.
source: At later (post-implantation) stages, Zfp281 expression was restricted to the epiblast and its derivatives (Figure 1A) and absent from the visceral endoderm (VE), a squamous epithelium derived from the PrE, which encapsulates the epiblast (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A and 1C

claim: Zfp281 is absent from the visceral endoderm (VE) at post-implantation stages.
source: At later (post-implantation) stages, Zfp281 expression was restricted to the epiblast and its derivatives (Figure 1A) and absent from the visceral endoderm (VE), a squamous epithelium derived from the PrE, which encapsulates the epiblast (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantitative fluorescence level comparisons of WT and Zfp281KO embryos

claim: No homozygous Zfp281 mutant mice were recovered at birth from intercrosses of heterozygous animals.
source: No homozygous mutant mice were recovered at birth from intercrosses of heterozygous animals, demonstrating a requirement for Zfp281 in embryonic development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data of live born pups shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Zfp281 mutant embryos die around E8.0.
source: The analysis of staged embryos revealed that mutants died around E8.0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data of embryos at different developmental stages shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: At E5.5, Zfp281KO embryos are recovered at Mendelian ratios and are indistinguishable from their WT and heterozygous littermates by gross morphology.
source: At E5.5, Zfp281KO embryos were recovered at Mendelian ratios and were indistinguishable from their WT and heterozygous littermates by gross morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: By E6.0–6.5, Zfp281 mutants become readily distinguishable from their WT littermates by their smaller size and distinct morphology, exhibiting a thickened VE layer.
source: However, by E6.0–6.5, Zfp281 mutants became readily distinguishable from their WT littermates by their smaller size and distinct morphology, exhibiting a thickened VE layer (Figure 1D, insets, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, insets with yellow bars).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and F-actin staining shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: Epiblast-specific loss of Zfp281 in tetraploid chimeras produces embryos with a comparable phenotype to that of constitutive gene ablation, with both types of mutant embryos exhibiting a thickened VE.
source: Epiblast-specific loss of Zfp281 produced embryos with a comparable phenotype to that of constitutive gene ablation, with both types of mutant embryos exhibiting a thickened VE (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by F-actin staining of tetraploid chimeras shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: 968 transcripts are significantly downregulated in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos at E6.5.
source: We identified 968 and 792 transcripts that were significantly downregulated and upregulated, respectively, in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 792 transcripts are significantly upregulated in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos at E6.5.
source: We identified 968 and 792 transcripts that were significantly downregulated and upregulated, respectively, in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Components of the Nodal signaling pathway (e.g., Nodal, Foxh1, Cripto, Lefty1, Lefty2) are significantly downregulated in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Among the significantly downregulated genes were components of the Nodal signaling pathway (e.g., Nodal, Foxh1, Cripto, Lefty1, Lefty2), and genes regionally-restricted in the epiblast and its derivatives (e.g., Fgf5, Otx2, Gsc) or the VE (e.g., Cer1, Lhx1, Dkk1, Hex, Hesx1) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Genes regionally-restricted in the epiblast and its derivatives (e.g., Fgf5, Otx2, Gsc) are significantly downregulated in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Among the significantly downregulated genes were components of the Nodal signaling pathway (e.g., Nodal, Foxh1, Cripto, Lefty1, Lefty2), and genes regionally-restricted in the epiblast and its derivatives (e.g., Fgf5, Otx2, Gsc) or the VE (e.g., Cer1, Lhx1, Dkk1, Hex, Hesx1) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Genes regionally-restricted in the VE (e.g., Cer1, Lhx1, Dkk1, Hex, Hesx1) are significantly downregulated in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Among the significantly downregulated genes were components of the Nodal signaling pathway (e.g., Nodal, Foxh1, Cripto, Lefty1, Lefty2), and genes regionally-restricted in the epiblast and its derivatives (e.g., Fgf5, Otx2, Gsc) or the VE (e.g., Cer1, Lhx1, Dkk1, Hex, Hesx1) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Afp, Patched1 (Ptch1), and Gsn are significantly upregulated in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: We also identified a number of genes that were significantly upregulated in mutant embryos, including Afp, Patched1 (Ptch1), Gsn (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The top enriched biological process for downregulated genes in Zfp281KO embryos is A-P axis specification.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis for the downregulated genes revealed the top enriched biological process to be A-P axis specification (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Nodal is the top-ranking signaling pathway enriched in the downregulated genes in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that Nodal was the top-ranking signaling pathway enriched in the downregulated genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA shown in Figure 2C

claim: Sox2 protein levels are unaffected in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Consistent with our RNA-seq data, we noted that Sox2 and Nanog protein levels were unaffected in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 3A,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or in tetraploid chimeras (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and 3D

claim: Nanog protein levels are unaffected in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Consistent with our RNA-seq data, we noted that Sox2 and Nanog protein levels were unaffected in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 3A,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or in tetraploid chimeras (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and 3D

claim: Oct4 protein is significantly downregulated in E6.25 Zfp281KO embryos.
source: In contrast, Oct4 protein was significantly downregulated in E6.25 Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3B and 3D

claim: Otx2 is expressed at significantly reduced levels in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Additionally, Otx2, which is activated during the naive-to-primed transition and critical for activation of epiblast gene-related enhancers (Buecker et al., 2014), was expressed at significantly reduced levels (Figure 3C,D) and mislocalized at the distal tip of mutant embryos, rather than being anteriorly restricted as in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3C and 3D, and WISH data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Otx2 is mislocalized at the distal tip of Zfp281KO embryos, rather than being anteriorly restricted as in WT.
source: Additionally, Otx2, which is activated during the naive-to-primed transition and critical for activation of epiblast gene-related enhancers (Buecker et al., 2014), was expressed at significantly reduced levels (Figure 3C,D) and mislocalized at the distal tip of mutant embryos, rather than being anteriorly restricted as in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Oct6 is downregulated in Zfp281KO embryos at early post-implantation stage.
source: This downregulation of Otx2 protein expression was already visible at an earlier stage in Zfp281KO embryos and in tetraploid chimeras, together with the downregulation of another marker of primed pluripotency, Oct6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), further indicating that epiblast maturation is defective in Zfp281KO embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: T protein is expressed in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: We noted that the T protein is expressed in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Cells that started expressing T had not downregulated Nanog in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: However, cells that started expressing T, had not downregulated Nanog (see inset in Figure 3E), indicating a failure in the extinguishment of pluripotency-associated genes as epiblast cells committed to differentiate in Zfp281KO embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E inset

claim: The domains of both T and Nanog expression in Zfp281KO embryos are proximally radialized, instead of being posteriorly restricted as in WT embryos.
source: The domains of both T and Nanog expression in mutant embryos were also proximally radialized, instead of being posteriorly restricted as in WT embryos (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Fgf8, Axin2 and Eomes are expressed and proximally radialized in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Analysis of RNA expression by wholemount mRNA in situ hybridization (WISH) of other markers of the primitive streak such as Fgf8, Axin2 and Eomes showed that, similarly to T, they were expressed and proximally radialized in mutant embryos (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C

claim: Levels of Fgf8 are reduced upon Zfp281 loss.
source: Our WISH and RNA-seq data both also revealed that levels of Fgf8 were reduced upon Zfp281 loss.
evidence: Supported by WISH and RNA-seq data

claim: T, Axin2 and Eomes RNA levels are not significantly reduced in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: However, T, Axin2 and Eomes RNA levels were not significantly reduced in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Hesx1, Dkk1, Cer1, Hex, and Lefty1 are absent or significantly reduced in expression in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: WISH of Hesx1, Dkk1, Cer1, Hex, and Lefty1 revealed their absence or significantly reduced expression in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Hex-GFP expression is reduced and distally-localized in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: In agreement with our WISH data, Hex-GFP expression was reduced and distally-localized, consistent with a failure in maintenance leading to impaired migration of the DVE/AVE population (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Hex-GFP reporter analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: The expression of proteins labeling the entire VE, such as Gata6, Lhx1 and Eomes, is unaffected in Zfp281 mutants.
source: By contrast, the expression of proteins labeling the entire VE, such as Gata6, Lhx1 and Eomes, was unaffected in Zfp281 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D

claim: The Nodal target and negative regulator Lefty2 is absent in the epiblast of Zfp281KO embryos.
source: By contrast, the Nodal target and negative regulator Lefty2 (expressed in the posterior epiblast of WT embryos) were absent in the epiblast of Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 4C), similarly to the related Lefty1 gene, which is expressed earlier in the VE, and also absent in mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Nodal and Eomes expression is radialized in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Nodal and Eomes are usually posteriorly localized in the epiblast at the site of the primitive streak (Nowotschin et al., 2013). However, their expression was radialized in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 4C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) while Nodal expression levels were reduced (Figure 2D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Nodal expression levels are reduced in Zfp281KO embryos.
source: Nodal and Eomes are usually posteriorly localized in the epiblast at the site of the primitive streak (Nowotschin et al., 2013). However, their expression was radialized in Zfp281KO embryos (Figure 4C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) while Nodal expression levels were reduced (Figure 2D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and WISH data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: EpiLCs (WT) express higher levels of lineage-specific genes than ESCs.
source: As expected, EpiLCs (WT) expressed higher levels of lineage-specific genes than ESCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Levels of expression of lineage-specific genes are reduced or abrogated in Zfp281KO relative to WT EpiLCs.
source: However, levels of expression of these genes were reduced or abrogated in Zfp281KO relative to WT EpiLCs (Figure 5A), indicating Zfp281 is important for establishing or maintaining expression of these genes during the transition.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Genes involved in Nodal signaling are similarly expressed in both WT ESCs and EpiLCs.
source: In addition, while genes involved in Nodal signaling were similarly expressed in both WT ESCs and EpiLCs, their levels of expression were downregulated in Zfp281KO versus WT EpiLCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with their downregulation in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Levels of expression of genes involved in Nodal signaling are downregulated in Zfp281KO versus WT EpiLCs.
source: In addition, while genes involved in Nodal signaling were similarly expressed in both WT ESCs and EpiLCs, their levels of expression were downregulated in Zfp281KO versus WT EpiLCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with their downregulation in Zfp281KO versus WT embryos (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Zfp281 binding is enriched at regions near gene transcription start sites (TSSs) and enhancers in both WT ESCs and EpiSCs.
source: To investigate how Zfp281 exerts transcriptional control of downstream target genes, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) with massively parallel sequencing (ChIP-seq) in both WT ESCs and EpiSCs, which revealed enrichment of Zfp281 binding at regions near gene transcription start sites (TSSs) and enhancers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), suggesting that Zfp281 is actively involved in transcriptional regulation in both naive and primed pluripotent states.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: There are 9358 common Zfp281 peaks in ESCs and EpiSCs.
source: There were 9358 common peaks for Zfp281, and 11,408 and 3467 peaks specific to ESCs and EpiSCs, respectively, which were lost and gained during the transition between these two states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting Zfp281 targets may be dynamically regulated during pluripotent state transition.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D

claim: There are 11,408 Zfp281 peaks specific to ESCs.
source: There were 9358 common peaks for Zfp281, and 11,408 and 3467 peaks specific to ESCs and EpiSCs, respectively, which were lost and gained during the transition between these two states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting Zfp281 targets may be dynamically regulated during pluripotent state transition.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D

claim: There are 3467 Zfp281 peaks specific to EpiSCs.
source: There were 9358 common peaks for Zfp281, and 11,408 and 3467 peaks specific to ESCs and EpiSCs, respectively, which were lost and gained during the transition between these two states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting Zfp281 targets may be dynamically regulated during pluripotent state transition.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D

claim: Promoters of lineage-specific genes such as T, Otx2, Eomes, Gsc are bound by Zfp281 with a higher enrichment in ESCs than in EpiSCs.
source: Surprisingly, promoters (Pro) of lineage-specific genes such as T, Otx2, Eomes, Gsc were bound by Zfp281 with a higher enrichment in ESCs than in EpiSCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Zfp281 binding intensities are reduced at promoters of T, Otx2, Eomes, and Gsc in EpiSCs compared to ESCs.
source: ChIP-qPCR analyses confirmed that Zfp281 binding intensities were reduced at these promoters in EpiSCs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Intensities of repressive histone mark H3K27me3 are diminished on promoters of T, Otx2, Eomes, and Gsc in EpiSCs compared to ESCs.
source: Consistent with the fact that these lineage-specific genes will be activated in primed cells, we also observed diminished intensities of repressive histone mark H3K27me3 on their promoters (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: There is no Zfp281 peak at promoters of Fgf5 or Fgf8.
source: By contrast, there was no Zfp281 peak at promoters of Fgf5 or Fgf8, indicating a promoter-independent regulation of Zfp281 on these two genes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Zfp281 binds at promoter-distal regions of Fgf5 and Fgf8 accompanied with increased H3K27ac in EpiSCs.
source: However, Zfp281 bound at promoter-distal regions of Fgf5 and Fgf8 (Figure 5E–F) accompanied with increased H3K27ac (Figure 5G) in EpiSCs, suggesting Zfp281 may be involved in enhancer activation on these two targets during the naive-to-primed transition.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E-G

claim: Zfp281 and Ep400 have the most similar binding patterns among epigenetic regulators and TFs in ESCs.
source: Hierarchical clustering analysis for ChIP-seq association revealed that Zfp281 and Ep400 have the most similar binding patterns.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq association analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Zfp281 and Ep400 show similar binding patterns with the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) components Ezh2 and Suz12.
source: Furthermore, Zfp281 and Ep400 also show similar binding patterns with the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) components Ezh2 and Suz12 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq association analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Zfp281 peaks are divided into two classes: (I) Zfp281/Ep400/Suz12-cobound, and (II) Zfp281/Ep400/Mbd3-cobound.
source: Zfp281 and Ep400 peaks exhibited a high correlation across the genome, but were mutually exclusive with Suz12 and Mbd3 peaks, dividing Zfp281 peaks into two classes: (I) Zfp281/Ep400/Suz12-cobound, and (II) Zfp281/Ep400/Mbd3-cobound (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq profiling shown in Figure 6B

claim: Class I Zfp281 target genes are highly enriched for GO terms that signify development.
source: Class I and Class II characterize the epigenetic features of target genes in ESCs, and are highly enriched for GO terms that signify development and pluripotency, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Class II Zfp281 target genes are highly enriched for GO terms that signify pluripotency.
source: Class I and Class II characterize the epigenetic features of target genes in ESCs, and are highly enriched for GO terms that signify development and pluripotency, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Class I genes are bivalent with a feature of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 co-enrichment.
source: The Class I genes are bivalent with a feature of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 co-enrichment (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq profiling shown in Figure 6B

claim: Zfp281's interaction with components of the PRC2 (Suz12) complex is reduced in EpiSCs compared to ESCs.
source: While we confirmed interactions of the PRC2 (Suz12) and NuRD (Chd4, Mbd3) complexes with Zfp281 in ESCs, we found their associations with Zfp281 were reduced in EpiSCs despite their expression levels being similar in the two populations (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Zfp281's interaction with components of the NuRD (Chd4, Mbd3) complex is reduced in EpiSCs compared to ESCs.
source: While we confirmed interactions of the PRC2 (Suz12) and NuRD (Chd4, Mbd3) complexes with Zfp281 in ESCs, we found their associations with Zfp281 were reduced in EpiSCs despite their expression levels being similar in the two populations (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Zfp281's interaction with components of the Tip60-Ep400 complex (Ep400, Trrap) is maintained in both ESCs and EpiSCs.
source: By contrast, Zfp281's interaction with components of the Tip60-Ep400 complex (Ep400, Trrap) was maintained in both ESCs and EpiSCs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Chromatin occupancy of Suz12 at bivalent promoters of T and Eomes is reduced in Zfp281KO relative to WT ESCs.
source: We confirmed the reduced chromatin occupancy of Suz12 at bivalent promoters of T and Eomes in Zfp281KO relative to WT ESCs (Figure 6D–E), indicating a Zfp281-dependent recruitment of PRC2 at the bivalent promoters.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D-E

claim: P-Smad2 is significantly reduced in Zfp281KO ESCs compared to WT ESCs.
source: P-Smad2 is significantly reduced in Zfp281KO ESCs compared to that in WT ESCs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Protein expression of Lefty significantly decreases by Zfp281 knockdown in EpiSCs.
source: P-Smad2 is not affected by Zfp281KD in EpiSCs, probably because of the Activin in culture constitutively activating p-Smad2. However, protein expression of the Nodal signaling target Lefty significantly decreased by Zfp281KD (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Zfp281 may directly regulate Lefty expression.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Zfp281 knockdown cells exhibit a strong phenotype of differentiation resistance to Activin/CHIR treatment.
source: The morphology of Zfp281KD cells revealed a strong phenotype of differentiation resistance, which is similar to that of ALKi treatment. Dome-shaped ESC-like colonies persisted in Zfp281KD cell cultures after Activin/CHIR treatment, a striking difference compared to WT control cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by phase images shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A

claim: Both Zfp281KD- and ALKi-treated cells exhibit decreased expression of the PS marker genes T and Lefty2.
source: RT-qPCR for up to 3 days after treatment indicated both Zfp281KD- and ALKi-treated cells exhibited decreased expression of the PS marker genes T and Lefty2 (a Nodal signaling target gene also expressed in PS) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C

claim: Zfp281 interacts with Oct4 and P300 in EpiSCs.
source: We first confirmed that Zfp281 interacts with Oct4 and P300 in EpiSCs (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Zfp281 co-localizes with Oct4 and P300 in almost all Zfp281 peaks.
source: Furthermore, ChIP-seq analysis indicates that Zfp281 co-localizes with Oct4 and P300 (Buecker et al., 2014) in almost all Zfp281 peaks (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting that Zfp281 may be involved in widespread relocation of Oct4 and P300, including both promoters and enhancers, in the naive-to-primed transition, that is independent of Otx2 association.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: Zfp281 localizes to characterized enhancers within the Nodal locus (PEE, NDE, HBE, but not ASE).
source: Zfp281 localizes to characterized enhancers within the Nodal locus (PEE, NDE, HBE, but not ASE, nomenclature from [Papanayotou et al., 2014]) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Zfp281 intensities are comparable between PEE and NDE, but decreased at HBE in EpiSCs compared to ESCs.
source: ChIP-qPCR analysis confirmed that Zfp281 intensities are comparable between PEE and NDE, but decreased at HBE in EpiSCs compared to ESCs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D

claim: H3K27ac intensity is reduced at HBE during the naive-to-primed transition.
source: It is reported that, during the naive-to-primed transition, Nodal enhancer activity relocates from the HBE to the ASE (Papanayotou et al., 2014). Indeed, H3K27ac intensity was also reduced at HBE (Figure 7E), consistent with reduced Zfp281 binding at this locus during the naive-to-primed transition (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Zfp281 exhibits high chromatin-binding activity at the HBE enhancer of the Nodal locus, as well as the regulatory regions within the Lefty2 and Foxh1 loci in E6.5 WT embryos.
source: Zfp281 exhibited high chromatin-binding activity at the HBE enhancer of the Nodal locus, as well as the regulatory regions within the Lefty2 and Foxh1 loci (Figure 7G), which would be abrogated in Zfp281 mutant embryos.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data on E6.5 embryos shown in Figure 7G

claim: Zfp281 is the first factor demonstrated to be critical in vivo for the exit from naive pluripotency in the embryo.
source: Notably, none of the pluripotency-associated factors, for which mouse mutants are available, have described phenotypes directly associated with the exit from naive pluripotency in the embryo. Zfp281 is the first factor demonstrated to be critical in vivo for this developmental transition; its loss results in embryonic lethality due to a failure in epiblast maturation.
evidence: Based on the absence of described phenotypes for other pluripotency factors and the demonstrated phenotype of Zfp281 mutants

claim: Loss of Zfp281 results in embryonic lethality due to a failure in epiblast maturation.
source: Notably, none of the pluripotency-associated factors, for which mouse mutants are available, have described phenotypes directly associated with the exit from naive pluripotency in the embryo. Zfp281 is the first factor demonstrated to be critical in vivo for this developmental transition; its loss results in embryonic lethality due to a failure in epiblast maturation.
evidence: Supported by the observed embryonic lethality and defects in epiblast maturation in Zfp281 mutants

claim: Zfp281 is concomitantly required for the initiation of expression of genes encoding Nodal signaling components and the lineage specification program during epiblast maturation.
source: Our data reveal that Zfp281 is concomitantly required for the initiation of expression of genes encoding Nodal signaling components and the lineage specification program during epiblast maturation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and WISH data showing downregulation of Nodal signaling components and lineage-specific genes in Zfp281KO embryos

claim: Zfp281 coordinates crosstalk among multiple epigenetic pathways through physical association with histone methylation (PRC2) and acetylation (Ep400, P300) complexes within epiblast cells.
source: Zfp281 coordinates crosstalk among multiple epigenetic pathways through physical association with histone methylation (PRC2) and acetylation (Ep400, P300) complexes within epiblast cells.
evidence: Supported by co-IP and ChIP-seq data showing interactions between Zfp281 and these complexes

claim: Crosstalk converges on the coordinated regulation of bivalent promoters and reorganization of enhancers leading to activation of lineage-specific genes and downregulation of pluripotency genes during the naive-to-primed transition.
source: Crosstalk converges on the coordinated regulation of bivalent promoters and reorganization of enhancers leading to activation of lineage-specific genes and downregulation of pluripotency genes during the naive-to-primed transition, arguing for a master regulator status of Zfp281 in controlling key molecular events leading to epiblast maturation (Figure 8, top panel).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing Zfp281 binding at bivalent promoters and enhancers, and changes in histone modifications

claim: Loss of Zfp281 results in a series of developmental defects within the epiblast, which non-cell-autonomously lead to a failure to establish or maintain the DVE/AVE resulting in A-P axis specification defects.
source: Accordingly, loss of Zfp281 results in a series of developmental defects within the epiblast, which non-cell-autonomously lead to a failure to establish or maintain the DVE/AVE resulting in A-P axis specification defects (Figure 8, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by WISH and immunostaining data showing defects in DVE/AVE markers and A-P axis specification in Zfp281KO embryos

claim: Afp is a pan-VE marker whose downregulation is coincident with the onset of gastrulation.
source: As we identified that Afp, a pan-VE marker whose downregulation is coincident with the onset of gastrulation (Viotti et al., 2014), is upregulated in our mutant embryos (Figure 2A,D), we speculate that Zfp281KO embryos may also fail in VE maturation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Viotti et al., 2014

claim: Zfp281KO embryos may fail in VE maturation.
source: As we identified that Afp, a pan-VE marker whose downregulation is coincident with the onset of gastrulation (Viotti et al., 2014), is upregulated in our mutant embryos (Figure 2A,D), we speculate that Zfp281KO embryos may also fail in VE maturation.
evidence: Based on upregulation of Afp in Zfp281KO embryos and the known role of Afp as a VE maturation marker

claim: Loss of Zfp281 binding at HBE may be a prerequisite for decommissioning the naive-specific Nodal enhancer in transitioning to the primed state.
source: In ESCs, HBE is bound by Oct4/Sox2/Nanog/Klf4 (Papanayotou et al., 2014), as well as Zfp281, however neither Zfp281 nor Oct4 binds ASE (Figure 7C), suggesting that loss of Zfp281 binding at HBE may be a prerequisite for decommissioning the naive-specific Nodal enhancer in transitioning to the primed state.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data showing Zfp281 binding at HBE but not ASE, and the known enhancer switching during naive-to-primed transition

claim: Nodal enhancer activity relocates from the HBE to the ASE during the naive-to-primed transition.
source: It is reported that, during the naive-to-primed transition, Nodal enhancer activity relocates from the HBE to the ASE (Papanayotou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Papanayotou et al., 2014

claim: Zfp281 may recruit Tet1 at Lefty1/2 promoters and maintain Lefty expression.
source: Our previous work indicated that Zfp281 physically interacts with Tet1 (Fidalgo et al., 2016), therefore Zfp281 may recruit Tet1 at Lefty1/2 promotors and maintain Lefty expression, suggesting a Nodal signaling-independent role of Zfp281.
evidence: Based on previous finding of Zfp281-Tet1 interaction and the role of Tet1 in maintaining Lefty1 expression

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are derived from, and represent an in vitro self-renewing counterpart of, the so-called 'naive' pluripotent epiblast cells of the blastocyst.
source: Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are derived from, and represent an in vitro self-renewing counterpart of, the so-called 'naive' pluripotent epiblast cells of the blastocyst (Nichols and Smith, 2009; Boroviak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nichols and Smith, 2009 and Boroviak et al., 2014

claim: Pluripotency comprises a continuum of states sequentially encompassing naive, formative and ultimately primed pluripotency.
source: Pluripotency comprises a continuum of states sequentially encompassing naive, formative and ultimately primed pluripotency (Smith, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith, 2017

claim: Upon blastocyst implantation into the maternal uterus, epiblast cells acquire characteristics of the more developmentally advanced formative and then primed states of pluripotency.
source: Upon blastocyst implantation into the maternal uterus, epiblast cells acquire characteristics of the more developmentally advanced formative and then primed states of pluripotency, which are represented by epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs) (Hayashi et al., 2011) and epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs) (Brons et al., 2007; Tesar et al., 2007; Kojima et al., 2014), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on EpiLCs and EpiSCs

claim: The transition to more developmentally advanced states of pluripotency occurs in the mouse embryo coincident with its implantation into the maternal uterus, at around embryonic day (E)4.5–5.0.
source: The transition to more developmentally advanced states of pluripotency occurs in the mouse embryo coincident with its implantation into the maternal uterus, at around embryonic day (E)4.5–5.0, and is marked by several stereotypical morphological and molecular changes (Bedzhov and Zernicka-Goetz, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bedzhov and Zernicka-Goetz, 2014

claim: Acquisition of the primed state of pluripotency precedes the onset of gastrulation (at E6.25).
source: Acquisition of the primed state of pluripotency precedes the onset of gastrulation (at E6.25), the process in which the three embryonic germ layers - ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm - are formed (Tam et al., 2006; Arnold and Robertson, 2009; Takaoka and Hamada, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on gastrulation

claim: Nanog, Klf4, and Rex1 (also named Zfp42) are highly expressed in the epiblast of the blastocyst and ESCs.
source: Nanog, Klf4, and Rex1 (also named Zfp42) are highly expressed in the epiblast of the blastocyst and ESCs, whereas Fgf5, Oct6 (also named Pou3f1), and Otx2 are upregulated in the epiblast following embryo implantation, or when ESCs differentiate toward EpiSCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pluripotency marker expression patterns

claim: Fgf5, Oct6 (also named Pou3f1), and Otx2 are upregulated in the epiblast following embryo implantation, or when ESCs differentiate toward EpiSCs.
source: Nanog, Klf4, and Rex1 (also named Zfp42) are highly expressed in the epiblast of the blastocyst and ESCs, whereas Fgf5, Oct6 (also named Pou3f1), and Otx2 are upregulated in the epiblast following embryo implantation, or when ESCs differentiate toward EpiSCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pluripotency marker expression patterns

claim: Eomes or T (also named Brachyury) are expressed in gastrulating embryos at the primitive streak and in EpiSCs.
source: Factors such as Eomes or T (also named Brachyury) are expressed in gastrulating embryos at the primitive streak (the site where pluripotent cells undergo lineage differentiation) and in EpiSCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lineage marker expression patterns

claim: Oct4, Sox2, and Zfp281 are expressed in the pluripotent epiblast throughout naive-to-primed state transitions.
source: Other pluripotency-associated TFs, such as Oct4, Sox2, and Zfp281, are expressed in the pluripotent epiblast throughout these state transitions, suggesting they may play distinct roles in different pluripotent states, or enable transitions between them.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pluripotency factor expression patterns

claim: Specific DNA modifications and reorganization of enhancer landscapes occur during the naive-to-primed transition.
source: Specific DNA modifications and reorganization of enhancer landscapes also occur during the naive-to-primed transition, together with genome-wide relocation of Oct4, as well as elevated binding of Otx2 and the P300 histone acetyltransferase at enhancers of genes specific to the primed state (Buecker et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buecker et al., 2014 and Yang et al., 2014

claim: Distal visceral endoderm (DVE) cells are critical for A-P axis establishment in the mouse embryo.
source: In the mouse embryo, distal visceral endoderm (DVE) cells, specified at the late blastocyst stage as a sub-population of the PrE, are critical for A-P axis establishment (Beddington and Robertson, 1999; Takaoka and Hamada, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beddington and Robertson, 1999 and Takaoka and Hamada, 2012

claim: At E5.5, DVE cells are localized at the distal tip of the embryo from where they migrate proximally towards the extra-embryonic/embryonic boundary, recruiting a second population (the anterior visceral endoderm or AVE) and defining an anterior to the embryo, thereby establishing an A-P axis.
source: At E5.5, DVE cells are localized at the distal tip of the embryo from where they migrate proximally towards the extra-embryonic/embryonic boundary, recruiting a second population (the anterior visceral endoderm or AVE) and defining an anterior to the embryo, thereby establishing an A-P axis (Stower and Srinivas, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stower and Srinivas, 2014

claim: The TGF-beta ligand Nodal, which is expressed by the epiblast, and several of its pathway components, such as Lefty1, Lefty2, Cripto, and Foxh1 are required for DVE/AVE specification, migration, and A-P axis formation.
source: The TGF-beta ligand Nodal, which is expressed by the epiblast, and several of its pathway components, such as the left-right determination factors (Lefty1 and 2) (Brennan et al., 2001), Cripto (also named Tdgf1) (Ding et al., 1998), and Foxh1 (Yamamoto et al., 2001) are required for DVE/AVE specification, migration, and A-P axis formation (Brons et al., 2007; Takaoka and Hamada, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on Nodal signaling components

claim: Ep400 is a component of the Tip60-Ep400 histone acetyltransferase complex that is necessary to maintain ESC self-renewal.
source: Ep400 is a component of the Tip60-Ep400 histone acetyltransferase complex that is necessary to maintain ESC self-renewal (Fazzio et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fazzio et al., 2008 and Chen et al., 2015

claim: Ep400 localization to promoters depends on H3K4me3, and Ep400 promotes histone H4 acetylation at both active and silent target promoters in ESCs.
source: A previous study showed that Ep400 localization to promoters depends on H3K4me3, and Ep400 promotes histone H4 acetylation at both active and silent target promoters in ESCs (Fazzio et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fazzio et al., 2008

claim: Bivalent genes remain silent in ESCs while undergoing fast activation in response to differentiation signals.
source: Bivalent genes remain silent in ESCs while undergoing fast activation in response to differentiation signals (Bernstein et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernstein et al., 2006
